:::{#thm-rank-dim}
#### The rank is the dimension of the column space

For any $m \times n$ matrix $\matr{A}$,

$$
\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = \dim\paren{\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})}.
$$

:::

::: proof

Let $r = \operatorname{rank}(\matr{A})$ (@def-rank),
and choose $r$ linearly independent columns of $\matr{A}$;
by @def-rank, no larger set of columns is linearly independent.
We show the chosen columns are a basis of $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ (@def-basis).

**Every column is in the span of the chosen columns.**
A chosen column is in that span trivially.
If some unchosen column $\vecf{a}_j$ were not in the span,
then adding it to the chosen columns would give $r + 1$ linearly independent columns
(@thm-add-outside-span),
more than $r$.
So every column of $\matr{A}$ is in the span of the chosen columns.

**The chosen columns span $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$.**
The span of the chosen columns is a subspace (@thm-span-subspace),
so it is closed under addition and scalar multiplication,
and it contains every linear combination of the columns of $\matr{A}$.
By @thm-column-space-span,
those combinations make up $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$,
so $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$ is contained in the span of the chosen columns.
The chosen columns are themselves columns of $\matr{A}$,
so their span is contained in $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$,
and the two sets are equal.

The chosen columns are linearly independent and span $\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})$,
so they are a basis of it,
and $\dim\paren{\mathcal{C}(\matr{A})} = r$ (@def-dimension).
If $r = 0$, every column is $\vzero_m$,
$\mathcal{C}(\matr{A}) = \cb{\vzero_m}$, and both sides are $0$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-rank-dim}
#### The rank of the matrix in @exm-column-space

For $\matr{A}$ in @exm-column-space,
$\mathcal{C}(\matr{A}) = \operatorname{span}\cb{(1, 3)}$ (@exm-column-space-span),
which has dimension $1$.
So $\operatorname{rank}(\matr{A}) = 1$, by @thm-rank-dim.
Directly: the first column $(1, 3)$ is linearly independent on its own,
and any two columns are dependent,
because each column is a multiple of $(1, 3)$.

:::
